thread:
alice: Heads-up — following the RFC, I sketched a small follow-up proposal for a lightweight "fence" API to coordinate cross-tier moves (GPU <-> host) and compaction. Wanted to get quick feedback before I turn it into an RFC proper.

ben: show me the sketch. does this change allocator responsibilities?

alice: short version: introduce an opaque 64-bit fence token that callers can attach to any allocation migration or compaction work. The runtime guarantees that once a fence is signaled, all in-flight uses from before the fence are drained. That gives compactor/evictor a clear handoff point without blocking hot-path alloc/free.

carla: sounds promising. how do we signal/observe efficiently from user threads? we can't make every generator wait on a syscall.

alice: agreed — signal is async. API: 
```
create_fence() -> u64
attach_fence(allocation_id, fence)
signal_fence(fence)
poll_fence(fence) -> bool
```
Attach is O(1) and just bumps an allocation's fence pointer. Poll is just reading a per-shard sequence number. No blocking syscalls on hot path.

dmitri: how does this interact with KV cache and prefix sharing? If two requests share KV but one is pinned for compaction with a fence, do we stall the whole stripe?

alice: design note: fences are per-allocation (granularity = allocation_id). KV cache entries reference allocations; cache eviction is allowed to choose alternatives. We explicitly avoid global stripe stalls by never making fence signaling an allocation-level write barrier for unrelated allocations. If shared KV spans fenced allocations, eviction may promote a copy or fallback to a read-through.

ben: who owns fence lifecycle? allocator or offloader?

alice: allocator owns fence attachment metadata (cheap pointer), offloader/compactor owns fence creation and signaling. Ownership rule: allocator must not block waiting for a fence to be signaled; it can return an error code (E_RETRY) if the allocation is being compacted/fenced. Offloader must use signal_fence when background migration safepoints complete.

eva: edgecases: what about partial writes (e.g., long-running kernels referencing portions of a tensor)? If kernel accesses continue after signal, we could corrupt.

carla: we treat kernel lifetime as a stronger pin: any dispatched GPU op that references an allocation implicitly increments a GPU-use counter; compactor must wait on both fence AND gpu-use==0. Fence only covers CPU-visible transitions/snapshots.

alice: exactly. Fence is a coordination primitive for the runtime's logical transitions (evict <-> resident), not a substitute for GPU synchronization primitives. We'll document that in the API surface.

dmitri: telemetry + debugging: how do we reason about stuck fences? can a misbehaving helper leak them forever and block compactions?

alice: plan is TTL+leak-detection: offload-bot emits metrics when a fence exists > X seconds and surface a stack snapshot of the creator. Also provide an unsafe_force_signal(fence) used by emergency tooling (requires admin perms).

ben: perf concerns: per-attachment atomic ops on hot allocs might add latency. Is the pointer bump in the allocator on the hot path cache-coherent?

alice: microbench: pointer bump is a single 64-bit store on allocation path. We avoid CAS in hot free path by using epoched slabs: attach only on heavyweight ops (compaction/async-migrate). For tiny allocations we leave fence=null.

carla: rollout plan? backward compat with older nodes in a cluster?

alice: default off. We'll gate with a runtime flag + version handshake in node bootstrap. New compactor will advertise fence-aware capability. Fallback: if node doesn't support fences, compactor falls back to existing stop-the-world handshake.

eva: TL;DR of tradeoffs please for the RFC intro:
- Pros: explicit, low-cost handoff marker; avoids global stalls; better observability for compaction leaks.
- Cons: additional metadata per alloc; complexity around kernel/GPU lifetime; requires orchestration changes for mixed-version clusters.

dmitri: +1 for trying. Can you add a short pseudocode example showing how compactor uses it in the RFC?

alice: will do. Example will show: create_fence -> attach all candidate allocs -> schedule background move -> wait poll_fence && gpu_use==0 -> signal -> retire old backing.

offload-bot: NOTE: compactor run scheduled in 10m window. Will report fence metrics after run. :robot_face:

carla: thanks — this makes the boundary between allocator, compactor, and evictor clearer. please add a few failure-mode tests (node crash while fence outstanding) to the RFC.

alice: yeah, adding crash/recovery and mixed-version tests. I'll open the RFC PR tomorrow. :thumbsup:
